The Basics ### What They Are Diodes are **nonlinear** devices. They conduct after the voltage reaches a forward threshold. For a silicon diode, the typical threshold is approximately 0.7 V. The exact threshold depends on the material. A diode blocks current in the opposite direction during normal operation. A diode is a **two-terminal device**: * **Anode (+):** Current enters this terminal. * **Cathode (-):** Current leaves this terminal. A stripe usually identifies the cathode on the package. During normal forward-biased operation, current flows from the **anode to the cathode**. * **PIV (peak inverse voltage):** This is the **maximum reverse-voltage rating** before reverse **breakdown**. If the reverse voltage exceeds the PIV, the diode enters breakdown. Current then flows backward from cathode to anode. This current often destroys the diode unless it is a Zener diode. ## 2. Common Circuit Uses ### A. Rectification Diodes are the main components in **half-wave** and **full-wave** rectifiers. These circuits convert alternating current (**AC**) into direct current (**DC**).

Standard full-wave bridge-rectifier configuration.

**How the Current Flows (Full-Wave Bridge):** A standard bridge rectifier contains four diodes. 1. **Positive half-cycle:** Diodes D2 and D3 become forward biased. Current flows through **D2 → load → D3 → ground**. 2. **Negative half-cycle:** The AC polarity reverses. Diodes D1 and D4 become forward biased. Current flows through **D4 → load → D1 → ground**. 3. **Result:** Current flows through the load in the **same direction** during both halves of the AC cycle. **Ripple and Filtering** * **Filter capacitors** connect across the load. They smooth the voltage "bumps," which are the voltage ripple after rectification. * **Voltage ripple** is the remaining output-voltage variation. The output is not perfectly flat DC yet. :::info Learn More For detailed information about conversion from AC to cleaner DC, see the **[Regulation Section](../../02-Power/Regulation/04-LDOs.md)**. ::: ### B. Clamping (Simple Protection) Diodes can operate as **voltage clamps**. When you take the output across a diode, the diode can limit a node. The limit is approximately one **forward-voltage drop above** the reference rail. **Electrostatic-Discharge (ESD) Steering Diodes:** You can protect slow control lines with **steering diodes** connected to the rails. Connect one diode to **ground (GND)** and one diode to **VCC**. * If a high-voltage spike reaches the line, the top diode conducts. It transfers the energy into **VCC**. * If a negative spike reaches the line, the bottom diode conducts. It pulls current from **GND**. :::warning Layout Note The power rails and [decoupling capacitors](<../01-Passives/02-Capacitors.md#bypass--decoupling>) must absorb the event energy. Keep the **traces short** and keep the ground-[return path](<../../05-PCB-Layout/02-Return-Paths.md#1-a-signal-needs-a-return>) tight. This arrangement is not ideal for high-speed signals because the diodes add capacitance. ::: ### C. RC Snubbers and RCD Clamps Fast switching of an inductive load can cause ringing and voltage spikes. Examples of inductive loads are motors and [transformers](<../02-Magnetics/01-Transformers.md#1-magnetic-coupling>). **1. RC Snubber (Damping)** An RC snubber contains a resistor and capacitor in series. It damps the ringing, which is an LC oscillation. The snubber also decreases the voltage rate of rise, dV/dt. * **Placement:** Connect the snubber across the switch or across the load. For a metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (**[MOSFET](<./03-MOSFETs.mdx#2-mosfet-operation-and-terminal-roles>)**), connect it across drain and source. **2. RCD Clamp (Peak Limiting)** RCD clamps are common in flyback converters. The diode operates as a check valve. It routes high-voltage spike energy into the capacitor. The capacitor holds the voltage. The resistor slowly converts the stored energy into heat. * **Components:** The diode routes energy. The capacitor holds voltage. The resistor dissipates heat. :::info Bench Tuning Snubbers 1. Measure the ringing frequency, fr. 2. Calculate the parasitic values: L × C ≈ 1 / (2π × fr)2. 3. Select the snubber capacitor: Csnub ≈ 3 × Cparasitic. 4. Select the snubber resistor: Rsnub ≈ √(L / Csnub). ::: ## 3. Diode Types ### Schottky Diodes Schottky diodes use a **metal-semiconductor** junction instead of a P-N junction. The junction usually contains platinum or tungsten on N-type silicon. **Why Use Them?** A Schottky diode does not have a P-N junction. As a result, it does not have minority-carrier injection. The diode turns off **immediately** and has zero reverse-recovery time. This behavior makes it ideal for high-speed switching regulators. * **Pros:** * **Lower forward drop:** The typical value is 0.2 V to 0.4 V. A silicon diode has a typical value of 0.7 V. The lower voltage causes less heat loss. * **Fast switching:** Schottky diodes are ideal for buck and [boost converters](<../../02-Power/Regulation/02-Boost%20Converter.md#1-step-up-conversion>) that operate from kilohertz (kHz) to megahertz (MHz). * **Cons:** * **High reverse leakage:** More current leaks through the diode when it is off. The leakage increases at high temperatures. * **Low breakdown voltage:** Schottky diodes with ratings greater than 100 V are difficult to find. ### TVS Diodes (Transient-Voltage Suppressors) **Transient-voltage-suppressor (TVS) diodes** are special avalanche diodes. They **turn on quickly** and **absorb short, high-energy events**. These events include ESD, lightning, and [inductive kickback](<../01-Passives/03-Inductors.md#interactive-the-inductive-kick>). * **Unidirectional:** This device operates like a Zener diode connected to ground. It blocks positive voltage until the clamp voltage occurs. It conducts freely for negative voltage. It is suitable for DC power lines. * **Bidirectional:** This device contains two back-to-back diodes. It clamps positive and negative spikes symmetrically. It is suitable for AC or data lines, such as [RS-485](<../../04-Digital-Interfaces/Serial-Buses/rs232-rs485.md#1-electrical-interfaces>). :::tip High-Speed Design For USB, HDMI, or [Ethernet](<../../04-Digital-Interfaces/Ethernet.md#1-mac-phy-and-cable>) interfaces, select **low-capacitance** TVS arrays. Place the array **at the connector**. Use a short ground path and one via directly at the pad. This layout minimizes stub length. ::: ## Worked example: solve the diode operating point A constant forward drop is useful for an initial estimate. An exponential model can refine the operating point when its parameters are known. Assume a 1 V source, a 1 kΩ series resistor, and a forward-biased diode to ground. Use n = 1, thermal voltage 25.9 mV, and saturation current 1 fA. The resistor gives I = (1 V − Vd) / 1 kΩ. The diode model gives I = Is × [exp(Vd / 25.9 mV) − 1]. Both equations must give the same current. One way to find the intersection is to alternate resistor-current and diode-voltage estimates. | Step | Assumed diode voltage | Resistor current | Updated diode voltage | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | 0 V | 1 mA | 0.71564 V | | 2 | 0.71564 V | 284.36 µA | 0.68307 V | | 3 | 0.68307 V | 316.93 µA | 0.68588 V | | Converged | Approximately 0.68567 V | Approximately 314.33 µA | Approximately 0.68567 V | The converged values satisfy the resistor and diode equations together. Extra decimal places describe the assumed model, not guaranteed device accuracy. This fixed-point iteration does not converge for every circuit. Bracketing methods provide a more reliable alternative when the residual is continuous and changes sign. Temperature, series resistance, and the chosen diode parameters can change the result. Compare the final model with the device data before using it for a design. ## LTspice example: half-wave rectifier import SpiceBatchSimulation from '@site/src/components/learning/SpiceBatchSimulation'; This example extends [rectification](#a-rectification) with an editable circuit and verified waveforms. The source supplies 12 V peak at 50 Hz. The source resistance is 10 ohms. The load resistance is 1 kilohm. The diode uses an embedded silicon teaching model. ### Reservoir charge and ripple Select the smallest capacitor to examine the rectified waveform. Its 1 pF value approximates a circuit without a reservoir capacitor. Select 47 or 220 microfarads to examine charge storage. The capacitor supplies the load when the source voltage cannot forward bias the diode. The output then falls until the next charging interval. A larger capacitor reduces this voltage change, which is called **ripple**. For a short charging interval, the approximate ripple is: **Ripple voltage = load current / (source frequency × capacitance).** This estimate assumes nearly constant load current. The resistor load and finite charging interval make the simulation result different from this estimate. Select the current plot to examine charging pulses. The diode supplies both the load current and the capacitor current during each charging interval. The peak diode current can exceed the average load current by a large factor. Source resistance limits this current in the example. ### Model scope The model includes forward voltage, series resistance, junction capacitance, and charge storage. It does not describe a particular production diode. Use the startup view to examine capacitor charging. Mean output and ripple use the final source cycle in the results table. ## LTspice example: full-wave bridge rectifier The bridge uses the same source, series resistance, load, and capacitor choices as the half-wave example. This makes the waveforms easy to compare. ### Follow both current paths The source floats between RAW and B. The series resistor connects RAW to A. The bridge output return is node 0. When A is positive relative to B, current flows through D1, the load, and D4. D2 and D3 block the other path. When B is positive relative to A, current flows through D2, the load, and D3. The load current keeps the same direction. Each conducting path contains two diode drops. Do not connect B to the output return in this circuit. ### Compare recharge frequency The reservoir capacitor receives charge on both input half cycles. A 50 Hz source produces a 100 Hz recharge frequency. The approximate ripple relation becomes: **Ripple voltage = load current / (2 × source frequency × capacitance).** At 47 microfarads, this example gives approximately 1.51 V peak-to-peak ripple. The half-wave example gives approximately 3.31 V with the same capacitor. The output averages differ because diode drops, load current, and charging intervals also differ. The bridge does not simply double the output voltage. Select the diode current plot to identify the alternating current paths. Compare [capacitor charge storage](#reservoir-charge-and-ripple) before examining a complete power supply. ### Simulation reference Both circuits use documented [LTspice device models](https://analogdevicesinc.github.io/ltspice-reference/ai_ref/CIRCUIT-ELEMENTS-REFERENCE.html). The downloadable validation records include current balance checks and a second simulation with smaller time steps. These checks verify numerical consistency, not physical component ratings.

--- title: BJTs and Amplifiers sidebar_label: BJTs --- import BJTBasicActive from '@site/src/components/BJTBasicActive'; import BJTFeedbackLoopDiagram from '@site/src/components/BJTFeedbackLoopDiagram'; import useBaseUrl from '@docusaurus/useBaseUrl'; # BJTs, Amplifiers, and Feedback ## 1. Basic BJT Idea
* A small **base current** controls a larger current from collector to emitter. * The base-emitter and base-collector junctions operate like diodes. **General NPN operating rules:** * If VC > VB and VBE ≈ 0.7 V, the transistor is in **active mode**. * If VBE > 0.7 V and VB > VC, the transistor is in **saturation**. * If VBE < 0.7 V, the transistor is in **cutoff**. You can use two analysis methods: * **General rule:** This method gives a quick hand analysis. It assumes values such as VBE ≈ 0.7 V. * **Ebers-Moll:** This exponential model gives a more accurate analysis. Use the general rule for most simple analyses. **General-analysis relationships:** * IC = β × IB Do **not** make a circuit depend on an exact value of β. The value can change by a very large amount. * VB ≈ VE + 0.7 V This relationship applies approximately when the transistor conducts. It applies in active mode and saturation. Otherwise, the transistor is in cutoff. * More base current causes more collector current. Sufficient base drive makes the collector-emitter path operate like a short circuit. This condition is saturation. * With no base current, the collector-emitter path operates like an open circuit. This condition is cutoff.
### Modes of Operation
**Active Mode** Active mode occurs when: * VB is approximately 0.7 V higher than VE. * VC > VB. You can bias the transistor at a selected operating point. This point is the **quiescent point (Q-point)**. The circuit operates around the Q-point. **Saturation** Saturation occurs when the base drive requests more collector current than the circuit can supply: IB × β > IC(maximum allowed by the circuit) In the simple model, IC = β × IB. The collector tries to draw more current than the circuit can supply. The voltage across the collector resistor continues to increase. Almost no voltage remains between collector and emitter. As a result, the collector voltage becomes very close to the emitter voltage. For an NPN transistor with a grounded emitter, VC ≈ 0 V. The base-collector junction becomes forward biased. The base-collector diode then conducts. **What Saturation Means:** * VCE becomes as close to 0 V as possible. * The transistor operates like a **closed switch** from collector to emitter. * All available current flows from the supply, through the load, and through the transistor. **Uses:** * You can use a saturated transistor as a **switch**. * To guarantee saturation, use sufficient IB. The condition IB × β > IC must remain true when β is low. * Do **not** use the exact value of β. Overdrive the base. **Cutoff** Cutoff occurs when VBE is not forward biased or IB ≈ 0. For an NPN transistor, ground the base or make VE > VB to get cutoff. **What Cutoff Means:** * Collector current does not flow. This statement ignores the small leakage current. * The terminals are effectively separate. The collector-emitter path is an open circuit. * The transistor operates like an **open switch**.
## 2. Ebers-Moll (Exponential Behavior)
**Important Ebers-Moll Formula:** * IC = IS × exp(VBE / VT) In this formula: * IS is the saturation current. It is very temperature dependent. * VT = kT/q is the thermal voltage. It is approximately 25 mV at room temperature. This formula shows that **VBE fundamentally sets IC**. Base current does not fundamentally set it. The relationship IC = β × IB is a result of this exponential behavior. **Inverse Relationship:** * VBE = VT × ln(IC / IS) Temperature affects VBE through both VT and IS. **Relationship Between Two Operating Points:** * IC2 / IC1 = exp(ΔVBE / VT) * As a result, ΔVBE = VT × ln(IC2 / IC1). **Internal Emitter Resistance, re:** * The small-signal emitter resistance is re = VT / IC. * At room temperature, re ≈ 25 mV / IC. Use amperes for IC. * If temperature or bias changes IC, then re also changes. * If the circuit uses only re for emitter resistance, small changes in IC cause **nonlinear** changes in gain and impedance.
## 3. Stability and Temperature
**Emitter Degeneration:** Add an explicit resistor, RE, in the emitter path. * Usually, make RE >> re. * Most emitter resistance then comes from a fixed resistor instead of the temperature-dependent re. If the circuit uses only re: * Linear changes in VBE do **not** cause linear changes in collector current. The relationship is exponential. * Changes in IC change re. As a result, impedance and gain also change. An external emitter resistor, RE, supplies **[negative feedback](<../../03-Signal-Modulation/Amplifiers/01-op-amps.md#negative-feedback>)**: * IC increases → IE increases → the voltage across RE increases. * VE increases → VBE decreases → IC is pushed down. This feedback helps prevent **thermal runaway**. During thermal runaway, temperature increases collector current. The higher current increases power dissipation, which causes a further temperature increase. **[Bypass Capacitor](<../01-Passives/02-Capacitors.md#bypass--decoupling>) Idea:** * Use a large RE for DC stability. **Bypass** the resistor with a capacitor for AC operation. * **DC:** The circuit sees RE. The resistor stabilizes the bias and opposes thermal runaway. * **AC:** The capacitor shorts RE. The AC gain is then set primarily by RC / re. * The AC signal has a direct path to ground. The circuit still uses RE to maintain stable DC bias. **Temperature-Dependent Parts:** * Temperature changes both VT = kT/q and IS. * The temperature dependence of IS is generally stronger and usually dominates.
## 4. Biasing Techniques
**Dual-Supply Biasing and [Voltage-Divider](<../01-Passives/01-Resistors.md#3-voltage-divider-and-loading>) Biasing** **Voltage-Divider Biasing:** * A resistor divider from one supply sets the base DC voltage. * A coupling capacitor lets the AC signal operate on top of this DC bias. * The signal can move around a mid-rail bias point and toward the supply rails. **Dual-Supply Biasing:** * The circuit has +VCC and -VEE. * You can bias the base and input signal at 0 V. * The signal can move symmetrically from +VCC to -VEE. * LTspice examples help you see this operation. **Using Two Resistors for High-Gain Applications** A single base-bias resistor can require a very low base voltage for a high-gain target. At this voltage, VBE can be very unstable. Two resistors can provide: * A more stable base bias through a voltage divider or feedback. * A method to set gain while the transistor stays in a better operating region. In some circuits, gain is related to a voltage ratio. The ratio uses the unbypassed emitter-resistor voltage and the collector voltage. You can think of this relationship as an **re voltage-divider idea**. **Collector-to-Base (Feedback) Bias** This is another bias method: * The current from the collector node, VC, sets VBE. * A resistor connects the collector to the base and supplies **DC feedback**. An example resistor value is 10 kΩ. * You can calculate the circuit so that the base settles approximately 0.7 V above the emitter. This action keeps IC approximately constant. * Select the 10 kΩ resistor so that its current supplies the necessary base current for Q1. * Matched transistors with the same VBE operate similarly at the same bias. For example, a collector voltage can put 0.8 V across a 10 kΩ resistor. This voltage sets base current. The base current sets IC. The collector current then sets VC and closes the feedback loop.
**[KVL](<../../00-Foundations/00-Foundations.md#circuit-theorems-analysis-tools>) with BJTs** When you calculate voltages and currents, include the approximate 0.7 V connection between base and emitter. * **NPN:** VB ≈ VE + 0.7 V. * **PNP:** VE ≈ VB + 0.7 V. * Include this voltage drop correctly in Kirchhoff's voltage-law (**KVL**) loops. ## 5. Amplifier Configurations
**Common-Emitter Amplifier** The **common-emitter amplifier** is another transistor application. * **DC output voltage:** Vout = VCC - IC × RC * **Approximate small-signal gain with an unbypassed RE:** Av ≈ -RC / RE * A more accurate gain calculation includes re and the bypass details. * The output is **180° out of phase** with the input. Basic DC and AC analysis shows the cause: * Base or emitter current increases → IC increases. * The voltage drop across RC increases → Vout decreases. **Emitter Follower (Common Collector)** The emitter follower has **high input impedance** and **low output impedance**. As a result, it can drive a relatively low-impedance load from a high-impedance source. It does not load the source excessively. **Key Relationships:** * Rin ≈ (β + 1) × RL. The load, RL, is connected at the emitter. * A simple emitter follower usually has no collector resistor. A collector resistor can cause transistor saturation. **Biasing and Bootstrapping:** * When a divider biases an emitter follower, do not use an extremely high divider impedance. * If divider impedance is too high relative to base input impedance, the bias becomes unstable. * **Bootstrapping** feeds part of the output back to the bias network. It can greatly increase **AC input impedance** without loading the signal. * The AC voltage at one resistor terminal moves with the output. Very little AC voltage then occurs across the resistor. * As a result, the effective AC resistance becomes very large. **Unity Phase Splitter (Transconductance-Amplifier Idea)** * In some topologies, the transistor operates as a **transconductance amplifier**. * The small-signal current-to-voltage ratio is gm = ΔIC / ΔVBE ≈ 1 / re. * A base-current or base-voltage change causes a collector-current change. * The collector-current change causes a collector-voltage change through RC. * Without RE, the emitter connects directly to ground. The general 0.7 V model can be inaccurate for small-signal operation. * Use the **Ebers-Moll model** and the small-signal parameters gm, rπ, and ro. **Differential Amplifiers and [CMRR](<../../03-Signal-Modulation/Amplifiers/02-differential-amps.md#2-common-mode-rejection-ratio>)** **[Differential Amplifier](<../../03-Signal-Modulation/Amplifiers/02-differential-amps.md#3-four-resistor-op-amp-difference-amplifier>):** * It amplifies the **voltage difference** between two points. * You can use it to measure across a component or between two integrated-circuit (**IC**) nodes. * An electrocardiogram (**ECG**) system uses LL, LA, RL, and RA electrodes. * Differential electrode outputs produce lead I, lead II, lead III, and other leads. * A differential amplifier removes noise that is common to both inputs. It primarily outputs the difference. **CMRR (Common-Mode Rejection Ratio):** * **CMRR** measures how well the amplifier rejects a signal that is **common** to both inputs. * CMRR is usually specified in decibels (**dB**). * High CMRR gives strong rejection of common noise. An example is 60 Hz hum on both ECG leads. **Transconductance (General Idea)** * **Transconductance** is the output-current change for an input-voltage change. * gm = ΔI / ΔV To describe circuit transconductance, ask: "How does the current change with respect to the input voltage?" For a BJT in the active region: * gm ≈ IC / VT
## 6. Current Sources and Mirrors
**Simple Transistor Current Source** Add a collector load and an emitter resistor to make a transistor current source. **Example:** * VE = VB - 0.7 V * IE = VE / RE = (VB - 0.7 V) / RE * For large β, IE ≈ IC. * As a result, IC ≈ (VB - 0.7 V) / RE. The current remains relatively constant while the transistor stays in active mode. This statement applies within the load limits. You can supply VB with a voltage divider. Make the divider impedance much less than β × RE. Changing VB produces a **voltage-controlled current source**. **Conceptual Resistive Current Source:** * Apply a voltage through a very large [source resistance](<../../00-Foundations/00-Foundations.md#the-ideal-source-and-the-real-source>). * If Rsource >> Rload, load-current change is small when the load changes. * Resistive current sources waste power. BJTs can supply current with less power loss. **Current Mirror** * A **current mirror** receives an input current and supplies a copy of that current. * You can use this circuit to replicate current into multiple loads. * It has **high output impedance**. This impedance keeps output current almost constant when output voltage changes. **Basic BJT Current-Mirror Example:** * Q1 has its emitter at +15 V. Its base is approximately 14.4 V, depending on the circuit. * Adjust the collector of Q1 to make its collector current the reference current. An example reference current is 1 mA. * Connect the bases and emitters of Q1 and Q2 together. The transistors then have the same VBE. * If Q1 and Q2 are matched, Q2 conducts approximately the same collector current. It supplies approximately 1 mA to its load. **Real Behavior:** Output impedance is not infinite. The mirrored IC can change if the load causes a very large output-voltage change. The current can also change if the load tries to draw too much current.
## 7. Advanced Configurations and Power
**Using a PNP Transistor** * Use a PNP high-side transistor when a grounded load must connect to a **positive supply**. * An NPN transistor is difficult to use in this high-side position. Its emitter must be at the supply. * The NPN base would have to be more than 0.7 V above the emitter. This voltage would exceed the supply. * You can cascade a PNP transistor with an NPN emitter follower. This arrangement removes the 0.7 V offset from one NPN emitter follower. **Darlington Configuration** * Two cascaded transistors operate like one transistor with **very high beta**. * βtotal ≈ β1 × β2 * The base-emitter voltage is approximately twice the normal value. It is approximately 1.2 V to 1.4 V. * **Disadvantage:** The configuration operates **slowly**. Q1 must turn off Q2, and stored charge can be large. * A resistor from the base of Q2 to its emitter can increase turn-off speed. **[Push-Pull](<../../03-Signal-Modulation/Amplifiers/01-op-amps.md#complementary-push-pull-output>), Crossover Distortion, and Amplifier Classes** **Push-Pull Output Stage:** This stage gives an output swing near the full positive-to-negative supply range. * **Positive half-cycle:** The NPN transistor, Q1, turns on. It supplies current to the load, such as a speaker. * **Negative half-cycle:** The PNP transistor, Q2, turns on. Its base is approximately 0.7 V below its emitter. * The PNP transistor lets current flow through the load in the opposite direction. **Crossover Distortion:** * Near 0 V, **both transistors are off**. Each transistor needs approximately 0.7 V of VBE to turn on. * This dead zone causes crossover distortion in the output waveform. **Correction for Crossover Distortion (Class AB):** * Add diodes D1 and D2 between the bases. Keep the diodes forward biased. * Each diode supplies approximately 0.6 V to 0.7 V. * This voltage pre-biases the transistors. At least one transistor is always slightly on. * This is a **Class AB amplifier** because both transistors conduct during a significant part of the cycle. * **Trade-off:** The transistors dissipate more power at idle because they are always partially on. * In this condition, the transistors operate like a type of voltage divider between the rails. **Class D Amplifiers:** * These **switching amplifiers** drive the output with high-frequency pulses. * Efficiency is very high because the transistors are usually fully on or fully off. * High-frequency switching causes more electromagnetic-interference (**[EMI](<../../05-PCB-Layout/High-Speed.md#eye-diagrams-and-interference>)**) emissions and requires filtering.
## 8. Negative Feedback and Stability
**Negative Feedback:** Negative feedback returns part of the circuit output to the input. The returned signal **opposes** the original signal. **Emitter-Resistor Example:** * IC increases → IE increases → VE increases. * VBE decreases → IC decreases. * This process stabilizes the circuit against temperature, transistor β, supply changes, and other variations. **Stabilized Operation and Thermal Runaway:** Negative feedback helps prevent **thermal runaway**. * Without stabilization: temperature increases → IC increases → power increases → temperature increases again. * With emitter degeneration, the feedback loop opposes this process and makes the circuit more stable. **Lower Output Impedance:** Negative feedback generally **decreases amplifier output impedance**. The output voltage then becomes less sensitive to load changes. **Gain-Stability Example:** If open-loop gain is A and feedback factor is B, closed-loop gain is: * ACL = A / (1 + A × B) When A × B is large: * ACL ≈ 1 / B As a result, B controls the gain. Resistors usually set B. Stable resistors produce more stable gain than temperature-sensitive transistors. **Voltage Feedback and Current Feedback** **Voltage Feedback:** * Subtract part of the **output voltage** from the input. * This action makes the voltage across the actual amplifier input very small. * The small input voltage requires very little current. As a result, **input impedance increases**. * The increase is often approximately the product of gain and feedback. **Current Feedback:** * Return part of the **output current** to the input so that it opposes the input. * The input voltage changes very little and remains almost constant. * The input can then accept more current. As a result, **input impedance decreases**.
## 9. BJTs Compared with FETs * Field-effect transistors (**FETs**) are very popular. * Metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors (**[MOSFETs](<./03-MOSFETs.mdx#2-mosfet-operation-and-terminal-roles>)**) dominate digital circuits and power switching. * BJTs can perform better than FETs in some analog applications: * **Accuracy:** An example is the predictable relationship between VBE and current. * **Low noise:** BJTs have low noise in some configurations. * **Higher transconductance:** At a specified current, a BJT has higher gm than a MOSFET. ## Output characteristic family import TransistorCurves from '@site/src/components/learning/TransistorCurves'; These illustrative curves show collector current versus collector-to-emitter voltage at three base currents. The active-region slopes represent finite output resistance. The low-voltage knee marks the approach to saturation. This drawing does not model breakdown or specify a real transistor's current rating. ## Worked example: loaded small-signal gain A small-signal model describes changes around a valid bias point. First establish the direct-current operating point and verify forward-active operation. Assume collector current Ic = 1 mA, thermal voltage Vt = 25.9 mV, and current gain beta = 100. Ignore the Early effect for this example. The transconductance is gm = Ic / Vt = 38.6 mS. The base-emitter resistance is rπ = beta / gm = 2.59 kΩ. Assume a 2 kΩ collector resistor and a 2 kΩ load. Their parallel resistance is 1 kΩ. With the emitter at signal ground, the gain from base voltage to collector voltage is approximately −gm × 1 kΩ = −38.6. A source resistance changes the voltage that reaches the base. Assume 1 kΩ source resistance and a bias network with negligible additional loading. The input divider gives 2.59 / (1 + 2.59) = 0.721. The gain from source voltage to output is approximately −27.9. ### Add emitter degeneration Now assume a 100 Ω emitter resistor remains unbypassed at the signal frequency. Keep the same collector current for comparison by adjusting the bias network. The resistance seen at the base becomes approximately rπ + (beta + 1) × Re = 12.69 kΩ. The collector load remains 1 kΩ. The base-to-output gain becomes approximately −beta × 1 kΩ / 12.69 kΩ = −7.88. Including the source resistance gives approximately −7.30. Degeneration reduces gain and increases input resistance. It also reduces sensitivity to transistor parameters within the model's valid range. These estimates exclude finite output resistance and high-frequency capacitance. Coupling and bypass capacitors must have suitable impedance at the operating frequency. Check output swing separately. A mathematically large gain does not prevent cutoff or saturation when the input amplitude increases. The distinction between bias and signal changes also appears in [state-space linearization](<../../03-Signal-Modulation/State-Space.md#7-equilibrium-and-local-linearization>). ## LTspice example: a basic BJT current mirror import CurrentMirrorSimulation from '@site/src/components/learning/CurrentMirrorSimulation'; This example expands the [current-mirror explanation](#6-current-sources-and-mirrors) with an NPN current sink. Its two emitters connect to ground. The reference resistor feeds Q1's joined collector and base. Q2 shares the base voltage, so matched transistors produce similar collector currents. ### What the curves show The reference current supplies Q1's collector current and both base currents. Q2 therefore does not copy the complete reference current exactly. With a 4.3 kΩ reference resistor, the simulated output current is approximately 0.9941 mA at 1 V. It rises to 1.0337 mA at 5 V. This rise illustrates the **Early effect**. The transistor's collector current depends on collector voltage as well as base-emitter voltage. At low output voltage, Q2 leaves forward-active operation. Its base-collector junction conducts, and the collector current can reverse near zero output voltage. The plot retains this negative current. The test voltage source can absorb current that arrives through the base-collector junction. ### Model and verification Both transistors use the same model: IS = 10 fA, BF = 100, and VAF = 100 V. The temperature is 27 °C. IS sets the transport saturation-current scale. BF sets the ideal maximum forward current gain. VAF is the forward Early voltage. These are illustrative model parameters, not specifications for a particular transistor. The example does not characterize mismatch, self-heating, or frequency response. The simulation passed connectivity, current-balance, and first-order calculation checks. A second run used half the voltage increment and tighter solver tolerances. The download includes the numerical results and validation record. See the [LTspice reference](https://analogdevicesinc.github.io/ltspice-reference/ai_ref/LTSPICE-QUICKSTART.html) for schematic and simulation file types. ## LTspice example: common-emitter amplifier import SpiceBatchSimulation from '@site/src/components/learning/SpiceBatchSimulation'; This circuit extends the [loaded small-signal gain example](#worked-example-loaded-small-signal-gain). A resistor divider sets the base bias from a 12 V supply. The input is a 10 mV peak sine wave at 1 kHz. Coupling capacitors separate the signal source and load from the transistor's DC bias. ### Separate bias from signal gain The emitter has a 100-ohm resistor in series with a 900-ohm resistor. Both resistors carry the DC emitter current. The bypass capacitor connects across only the 900-ohm resistor. It changes the alternating-current path while the total DC emitter resistance stays at 1 kilohm. With a 1 pF bypass, the capacitor has negligible effect at 1 kHz. The gain magnitude is approximately 3.00 V/V. With a 100-microfarad bypass, the capacitor bypasses most of the 900-ohm resistance at 1 kHz. The gain magnitude increases to approximately 25.53 V/V. The 100-ohm resistor remains in the signal path. This remaining [emitter degeneration](#add-emitter-degeneration) limits gain and reduces sensitivity to transistor parameters. ### Understand the intermediate case The 1-microfarad capacitor does not provide a complete bypass at 1 kHz. Its impedance changes both gain and phase. The simulated gain magnitude is approximately 14.35 V/V. The output phase is approximately −133.56 degrees relative to the input. For the large capacitor, output phase is approximately −179.12 degrees. The result is close to the familiar inverted output of a common-emitter stage. ### Check the operating point The mean collector voltage remains approximately 7.57 V for all three capacitor values. The transistor remains in its forward-active region throughout these runs. A larger input can cause clipping, but these runs use a small signal. They isolate the effect of emitter bypass on gain and phase. The embedded model includes finite current gain, output resistance, and junction capacitance. It does not establish the limits of a production transistor. The results table uses the final ten signal periods. The downloaded CSV preserves the original simulation samples and restores the simulator's time offset.

before: --- title: FETs (MOSFETs and JFETs) sidebar_label: FETs --- import useBaseUrl from '@docusaurus/useBaseUrl'; import MosfetCalc from '@site/src/components/MosfetCalc'; # Field-Effect Transistors (FETs) ## 1. Fundamentals and Device Types **Core Concept** A field-effect transistor (**FET**) is a voltage-controlled current source. This page covers metal-oxide-semiconductor FETs (**MOSFETs**) and junction FETs (**JFETs**). In the ideal model, the **gate** draws zero direct current (**DC**). As a result, the input impedance is infinite. A real gate has small leakage current and capacitance. Current flows briefly when the gate charges or discharges during switching. **Key Definitions** * **Gate-source voltage, VGS:** This is the control voltage. It changes the channel conduction. You can think of it as a valve control. * **Drain-source voltage, VDS:** This voltage drives current through the channel. You can think of it as pressure across the channel. * **Threshold voltage, Vth:** This is the specified VGS where an enhancement channel starts to form. * **Zero-gate drain current, IDSS:** This is the specified JFET or depletion-device current at VGS = 0. The original notes describe IDSS as the maximum zero-bias current. A depletion MOSFET can conduct more current when positive gate drive is permitted. **Core Equations** For a simplified square-law MOSFET in saturation: * ID = k × (VGS - Vth)2 The original rough current-to-voltage ratio is ID / VGS. The small-signal definition of **transconductance** is: * gm = dID / dVGS For the simplified square-law model: * gm = 2ID / (VGS - Vth) For an unloaded common-source stage: * Av ≈ -gm × RD **Enhancement and Depletion Devices** **Enhancement Mode (Normally Off):** * If VGS < Vth, no strong channel exists. In the ideal model, IDS = 0. * Apply gate bias to turn the device on. * Enhancement MOSFETs are standard devices for logic and power applications. **Depletion Mode (Normally On):** * A channel exists at VGS = 0. * For an N-channel device, negative gate bias decreases the current and can stop it. * The specified zero-bias current is IDSS. ## 2. MOSFET Operation and Terminal Roles ### N-Channel Operating Regions The following boundaries use the ideal long-channel model. 1. **Cutoff (Open Switch)** * **Condition:** VGS < Vth. * **Result:** IDS ≈ 0. The switch is **off**. * A real device can have a small leakage current. 2. **Ohmic or Linear Region (Resistor)** * **Condition:** VGS > Vth and VDS < VGS - Vth. * **Behavior:** The device operates as a voltage-controlled resistor. * For small VDS, drain current increases approximately linearly with VDS. The basic relationship is I = V/R. * **Uses:** Variable resistance and low-loss power switching. 3. **Active or Saturation Region (Current Source)** * **Condition:** VDS ≥ VGS - Vth. * **Behavior:** The device operates approximately as a constant-current source. * The channel is pinched off near the drain. * In the ideal model, a further increase in VDS does not increase current. * Gate drive, VGS, primarily sets the current. * A real device has some current change because of channel-length modulation. ### Source and Drain Design Intuition Some small-signal FET structures are approximately symmetrical. In those devices, terminal voltage can determine the effective source and drain. * **N-channel source:** The lower-voltage channel terminal operates as the source. * **P-channel source:** The higher-voltage channel terminal operates as the source. Power MOSFETs are not fully symmetrical. Their body connection and intrinsic body diode give the terminals a fixed practical orientation. ### Negative-Drain Trap Consider an N-channel MOSFET that switches a signal line to ground. 1. You assume that the drain is the high-side terminal. 2. You set the gate to 0 V to turn the MOSFET off. 3. The signal line then decreases to -2 V. 4. That terminal is now below the grounded terminal. 5. It becomes the effective source in a symmetrical small-signal device. 6. The gate-source voltage becomes: VGS = VG - Vtrue source = 0 V - (-2 V) = +2 V 7. The FET can turn on unintentionally. To keep the device off, make the gate more negative than the most-negative signal. Also check the body-diode path in a practical MOSFET. ## 3. JFET and Depletion-Mode Operation Junction field-effect transistors (**JFETs**) are **normally on**. Their zero-bias behavior is the reverse of an enhancement MOSFET. **How an N-Channel JFET Operates** * At 0 V gate bias, current is approximately IDSS. * A more-negative gate voltage narrows the channel and eventually pinches it off. * The gate is a diode junction to the channel. * **Do not forward bias the gate.** For an N-channel JFET, do not make the gate positive relative to the source. * Forward bias causes gate current and can damage the device. **JFET Compared with a Depletion MOSFET** * **Similarity:** Both devices are normally on. Negative VGS decreases N-channel current. * **Difference:** A depletion MOSFET has an insulated gate. * You can drive a depletion-MOSFET gate positive to get more current without forward-biasing a gate junction. * JFETs are useful for **low-noise** linear circuits, audio front ends, and amplifiers. * JFETs have no thin gate-oxide layer. As a result, they are generally less susceptible to electrostatic-discharge damage than MOSFETs. ## 4. Basic Applications ### High-Impedance Buffers and Source Followers Use a FET when bipolar-junction-transistor (**BJT**) input current would load the signal source. The approximate source-follower gain is: * Av = 1 / [1 + 1 / (gm × RL)] The approximate output impedance is 1/gm. Because gm changes with signal current, output impedance also changes. The original notes call this change a "wobble." It can cause distortion. Use a constant-current-source load or a negative supply to stabilize the operating point. ### Analog Switches FETs in the **ohmic region** operate as low-resistance switches. Applications include multiplexers and [sample-and-hold](<../../03-Signal-Modulation/Data-convertes/Sample-holding.md#1-basic-circuit>) circuits. ### Variable Resistors In the ohmic region, a change in VGS changes RDS. You can use this effect for voltage-controlled volume. Device range and distortion limit this application. ### Power Switching MOSFETs dominate many power-switching applications because RDS(on) can be low. Their resistive on-state and positive temperature coefficient make parallel operation comparatively easy. ## 5. Analog Signal Switching This section gives detailed requirements for FET audio and data switches. ### Feedthrough An ideal off switch is an air gap. A real MOSFET has **drain-source capacitance, Cds**. * **Effect:** High-frequency signals can cross this capacitance when the switch is off. The unwanted signal then appears at the output. * **Solution:** Use a T-switch or single-pole, double-throw (**SPDT**) arrangement. Ground the signal path when the switch is off. ### Floating Output and Ghost Signals A floating, high-impedance output can receive noise and leakage signals. * **Resistor solution:** Add a load resistor from the output to ground. A typical starting range is 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ. * **Low-value example:** A 1 kΩ resistor decreases feedthrough. It also forms a divider with Ron and causes signal loss. * **High-value example:** A 1 MΩ resistor causes little signal loss. It can be too weak to discharge capacitive leakage. * **Preferred solution:** Use a second switch or an SPDT switch. Actively ground the output when the signal is disconnected. ### CMOS Transmission Gate A complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (**CMOS**) transmission gate uses two device types. **Problem:** 1. An N-channel MOSFET passes a low voltage well. 2. As its source voltage increases, VGS decreases. 3. The device then passes a high voltage poorly and can turn off. 4. A P-channel MOSFET has the complementary behavior. **Solution:** * Connect an N-channel MOSFET and a P-channel MOSFET in parallel. * One device handles low voltages, and the other handles high voltages. * The pair permits **rail-to-rail** signal switching. ### Distortion and Charge Injection * **Total harmonic distortion (THD):** Ron changes as signal voltage changes. The effective VGS also changes. This nonlinear resistance causes distortion. * **[Charge injection](<../../03-Signal-Modulation/Data-convertes/Sample-holding.md#charge-injection-and-pedestal-error>):** Gate capacitance stores charge. When the switch turns off, some charge can enter the signal path and cause a voltage spike. * **Correction:** Use an analog-switch integrated circuit (**IC**) that specifies low charge injection. ## 6. Current Sinks and Sources A **current sink** draws a specified current. A **current source** supplies a specified current. An ideal circuit keeps this current constant for all node voltages. A real circuit does this only within its compliance-voltage range. ### Why Use a Current Sink? Assume that an [emitter follower](<./02-BJTs.md#5-amplifier-configurations>) must supply a fixed current, X. * **Resistor method:** Connect a resistor to the negative rail. This method uses more power and decreases input impedance. * **Active-sink method:** Use a JFET or BJT. An active device maintains higher impedance and better current control. ### JFET Current-Sink Example A JFET is a normally-on depletion device. As a result, you can use source resistance for self-bias. **Self-Bias Sequence:** 1. Tie the gate to -12 V. 2. The source voltage is -12 V + ID × RS. 3. The result is: VGS = VG - VS = -12 V - (-12 V + IDRS) = -IDRS 4. Select RS to produce the necessary negative VGS. 5. For a 5 mA design: RS = |VGS(required)| / 5 mA **JFET-Sink Limitation:** IDSS can change greatly between parts. As a result, JFET current can be difficult to predict. A JFET sink is usually not consistent enough for a tight tolerance. Use a BJT sink when the application needs better predictability. ### BJT Current Sink and Mirror * **Concept:** Set collector current by setting a fixed emitter current. * **Benefit:** The circuit does not require an exact VBE bias. Collector current is approximately equal to the selected emitter current. * **Common-emitter application:** An emitter current sink keeps IE almost constant. As a result, IC is also almost constant. * The collector DC voltage is: VC ≈ VCC - Isink × RC This method decreases bias dependence on transistor β and VBE. ## 7. Hybrid and Advanced JFET Circuits ### JFET-BJT Series-Feedback Pair This circuit combines a **JFET** high-input-impedance stage with **BJT** gain and output stages. **Block 1: JFET Input Stage** * **Function:** Supplies extremely high input impedance. * **Current:** Source resistor R2 sets ID. **Block 2: BJT Q2 Gain Stage** * **Function:** Supplies high voltage gain. * **Bias:** R3 sets the collector bias current. * **Approximate gain:** gm × Rload. **Block 3: BJT Q3 Emitter-Follower Output Stage** * **Function:** Supplies high input impedance and low output impedance. * Q3 draws very little current from Q2. * Without Q3, a load such as 3.3 kΩ is in parallel with the Q2 collector load. This condition greatly decreases gain. * With Q3, the load is isolated. Q2 sees high impedance, and gain increases greatly. ### Hybrid JFET and Op-Amp Amplifier **Open-Loop Analysis Without Rf:** * Bias the JFET. An alternating-current (**AC**) drain current, ID, then flows. * The [op-amp](<../../03-Signal-Modulation/Amplifiers/01-op-amps.md#1-op-amp-fundamentals>) operates as a current-to-voltage converter. * The original notes write Vout = gm × Rgain. Dimensionally, this product is the voltage-gain magnitude. * The voltage relationship is: Vout = Vin × gm × Rgain **Numerical Example:** * gm = 25 mS. * R = 100 kΩ. * Gain is 2500. * A 1 mV input produces a 2.5 V output. **Closed-Loop [Negative Feedback](<../../03-Signal-Modulation/Amplifiers/01-op-amps.md#negative-feedback>):** 1. Input voltage increases. 2. VGS moves closer to 0 V. 3. The JFET conducts more current. 4. The op-amp output increases. 5. Current into the JFET source increases. 6. Source voltage increases. 7. Gate and source voltages then increase together. 8. As a result, VGS remains almost constant. The feedback-resistor ratio, Rf / Rg, sets the closed-loop gain. Transistor parameters no longer set it directly. ### JFET Differential Amplifiers **Circuit A: Resistive Load** * A current sink sets the total current for the pair. * If VQ1 > VQ2, Q1 draws more current. * Because total current is fixed, Q2 must draw less current. * The D1 voltage decreases, and the D2 voltage increases. * The circuit amplifies this difference. * In an ideal matched pair, a 1 V increase at both inputs causes no differential-output change. * Limitations are low gain and part-to-part gm variation. **Circuit B: Active Load** * A BJT [current mirror](<./02-BJTs.md#6-current-sources-and-mirrors>), Q3 and Q4, replaces the drain resistors. * The mirror operates as a high-resistance constant-current source. * Gain is Av = gm × Rload. * The mirror has high output resistance. As a result, it increases gain significantly. ### JFET Differential Amplifier with Feedback 1. A current sink, such as 10 mA, sets the total pair current. 2. At Vin = 0, Q1 and Q2 each conduct 5 mA. 3. The differential output is zero. 4. If the Q1 input increases, Q1 conducts more current. 5. Q2 then conducts less current. 6. The circuit amplifies the current difference. 7. Negative feedback limits this difference to a manageable gain. 8. Feedback also stabilizes the circuit against gm variation. ## 8. Gate-Drive Dynamics Gate-drive behavior is important in switching circuits, motor drivers, and power supplies. ### Static Gate Current * **Ideal:** The gate is isolated by an oxide or another insulator. The "glass" analogy describes this insulation. In the ideal model, IG = 0. * **Real:** Small leakage current exists. It can be in the picoampere range. * **Protection devices:** Some discrete MOSFETs include Zener or other electrostatic-discharge protection. These devices can leak nanoamperes or microamperes. * **Design rule:** Check the datasheet before you use a protected MOSFET in an ultra-high-impedance electrometer circuit. ### Dynamic Gate Current Use a **bucket or capacitor analogy** for the gate. * **DC:** After the gate capacitance charges, drive current stops except for leakage. * **Turn-on:** The driver must put charge into the gate. * **Turn-off:** The driver must remove charge from the gate. * **Average switching-current relationship:** I = Qgate / time. **Example:** * [Gate charge](<../../02-Power/Power%20Control/Gate-Drivers.md#1-gate-charge-and-switching>) is 50 nC. * Necessary switching time is 100 ns. * Required current is 50 nC / 100 ns = 0.5 A. Use a dedicated **gate-driver IC** to supply these short high-current pulses. A standard 20 mA general-purpose input/output (**[GPIO](<../../04-Digital-Interfaces/Embedded-Systems.md#pins-and-external-circuits>)**) pin is too weak for fast switching in this example. ### Miller Plateau During gate charging, gate voltage first increases, then becomes almost constant, and then increases again. 1. **Region 1: Charge CGS** * Gate voltage increases approximately linearly. * The MOSFET is off. 2. **Region 2: Miller Plateau** * The MOSFET turns on, and drain voltage decreases. * The changing drain voltage moves charge through gate-drain capacitance, Cgd. * Driver current continues, but gate voltage stays almost constant. * The feedback capacitance uses the supplied charge during this interval. 3. **Region 3: Complete the Gate Charge** * The drain transition is complete. * The device moves toward the fully enhanced ohmic on-state. * Gate voltage increases to the driver level. During the plateau, the MOSFET is partially on and operates as a resistor. It dissipates heat. Supply sufficient gate current to move through the plateau quickly. ## 9. Power MOSFET Design This section gives requirements for high-current devices. ### Thermal Stability of RDS(on) * RDS(on) increases with temperature. This is a positive temperature coefficient. * In the fully enhanced switching state, a hot die area develops more resistance. * Current then moves toward cooler die areas. * This behavior gives a sharing advantage relative to BJTs and makes parallel MOSFET operation easier. * Calculate power dissipation with the worst-case resistance. * At 125°C, resistance can be 1.5 times its specified 25°C value. This sharing benefit does not remove the linear-mode hot-spot risk described later. ### Body Diode * A power MOSFET has an intrinsic P-N body diode between its source and drain. * In a suitable circuit orientation, this diode can carry [inductive flyback](<../01-Passives/03-Inductors.md#interactive-the-inductive-kick>) current. * This path can prevent damaging drain-source overvoltage. * The body diode can have slow reverse recovery. * Slow diode turn-off can cause [shoot-through](<../../02-Power/Power%20Control/Gate-Drivers.md#4-high-side-drive-and-dead-time>) current in an [H-bridge](<../../02-Power/Power%20Control/Motor-Drives.md#drive-paths-and-braking>). * Select a device with suitable fast-recovery behavior when the application requires it. ### Safe Operating Area The safe-operating-area (**SOA**) graph shows safe combinations of VDS and ID. Designers sometimes call this graph the datasheet "map of death." **Linear-mode warning:** A switching MOSFET can be a poor variable resistor. Local die hot spots can cause failure inside the calculated total-power limit. ### Ways to Damage a MOSFET 1. **Resistive Heating from Insufficient Gate Voltage** * **Cause:** Apply 3.3 V to a gate that requires 10 V for low RDS(on). * **Result:** The FET does not turn fully on. * RDS stays high, and I2R heating can destroy the device. 2. **Inductive Overvoltage** * **Cause:** Turn off a motor or [solenoid](<../../02-Power/Power%20Control/Motor-Drives.md#electrical-and-mechanical-behavior>) quickly without a [snubber](<./01-Diodes.md#c-rc-snubbers-and-rcd-clamps>) or clamp. * **Result:** Inductor current forces voltage to increase until a clamp, breakdown path, or parasitic path conducts. * Excess voltage can puncture device insulation and destroy the MOSFET. ### High-Side Floating Gate **Scenario:** A ground-referenced logic signal must control a high-side N-channel MOSFET. **Technique:** Use a discrete current source that pushes current against a gate-source resistor. This circuit lets the gate-control voltage move upward with the source voltage. An integrated **high-side driver** performs essentially this function internally. ## 10. Real-World Limitations and Selection ### FET "Softness" Compared with BJT "Stiffness" At a specified current, BJTs usually have higher gm than FETs. As a result, a BJT follower usually has lower output impedance. The original notes call the BJT output "stiff" and the FET output "soft." * Approximate follower output impedance is 1/gm. * A FET follower usually has higher output impedance than a BJT follower at the same current. * As a result, its output voltage changes more when load current changes. * At extremely low currents, the difference becomes smaller. ### Precision Current Setting * MOSFET VGS(th) can differ by as much as 3 V between devices in the same batch. * As a result, a fixed gate voltage cannot set an accurate drain current. * BJT VBE at a specified current is more predictable, but approximately 0.7 V is not an exact constant. * BJTs usually give better results in high-precision discrete current mirrors and sources. ### Miller Effect and Bandwidth * A high [source impedance](<../../00-Foundations/00-Foundations.md#the-ideal-source-and-the-real-source>) decreases bandwidth when it interacts with Miller capacitance. * The capacitance and source impedance make a low-pass network. * Higher source impedance decreases the cutoff frequency. * Use a **cascode** to isolate the input device from large output-voltage changes. ### Cascode * Put a common-gate FET above a common-source FET. * The upper device keeps the lower-device drain voltage almost constant. * This arrangement greatly decreases the Miller effect. * It also greatly increases output impedance. ## 11. Linear Examples and the Danger Zone The original Art of Electronics note gives this guidance: discrete MOSFETs can make linear amplifiers, but they are frequently not the best choice. ### Discrete-MOSFET Variability and Noise A device such as the 2N7000 is less predictable than a BJT or JFET in a precision linear circuit. * **Threshold variation:** Vth can range from 0.8 V to 3 V in one batch. * A precise DC bias point is not possible without feedback. * **Noise:** Generic MOSFETs can have higher low-frequency 1/f noise than JFETs in audio applications. * Popcorn noise is a separate burst-noise mechanism. Do not use it as another name for 1/f noise. * Use a JFET or BJT for a low-noise microphone preamplifier. Do not select a generic MOSFET without a noise evaluation. ### CMOS Inverter Linear-Amplifier Method This is an unconventional low-cost method. The original notes call it a "MacGyver" method. * A CD4069 or 74HCU04 digital inverter contains a P-channel FET above an N-channel FET. * Connect a high-value resistor, such as 1 MΩ, from output to input. * This resistor makes the inverter self-bias at VDD / 2. * The inverter then operates as a high-gain linear amplifier. * **Warning:** Use an **unbuffered** U-series device. * A buffered inverter has too much gain and can oscillate. ### Discrete-MOSFET Current-Mirror Matching * **Theory:** If the gates are connected, equal gate-source voltage should produce equal currents in matched devices. * **Reality:** Two discrete MOSFETs from one bag can differ in Vth by 0.5 V. * One device can conduct 1 mA while the other conducts 10 mA. * **Correction:** Use a matched pair on one die. The CD4007 is one example. * BJTs are more tolerant of discrete-device variation in this application. ### Linear-Power Hot Spots This problem occurs when a MOSFET operates as a variable resistor in a linear regulator or Class A amplifier. * Modern switching MOSFETs are optimized for high cell density. * With high voltage and high current at the same time, current can concentrate in a small die area. * This concentration causes localized thermal runaway. * The MOSFET can fail below its total power rating. * Use a linear-rated MOSFET, frequently made with older planar technology. * Also check the **DC line** on the SOA graph. ## Geometry and the body connection The **width-to-length ratio (W/L)** describes channel geometry in a simple MOSFET model. Greater width can increase current capability and gate capacitance. A shorter channel can increase current for the same bias in a long-channel approximation. Short-channel effects limit direct use of that approximation in modern devices. Discrete power MOSFETs usually connect the body to the source internally. This controls body potential and helps suppress unwanted parasitic transistor operation. Integrated MOSFET bodies can use a shared well connection. Their body voltage can change threshold through the body effect. Do not assume every body is separately accessible. Gate oxide is thin and tolerates limited electric field. Check gate-to-source limits even when drain voltage remains within its rating. ## Output characteristic family import TransistorCurves from '@site/src/components/learning/TransistorCurves'; These curves use an ideal long-channel model with a 1 V threshold and a 1 mA/V² model factor. They exclude channel-length modulation and breakdown. The linear region ends when drain-to-source voltage equals gate overdrive. The saturation current then remains constant in this simplified model. See [MIT MOSFET and CMOS operation](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c3/c3s1/) for the model's circuit context. ## LTspice example: JFET self bias import SpiceBatchSimulation from '@site/src/components/learning/SpiceBatchSimulation'; This circuit extends [JFET operation](#3-jfet-and-depletion-mode-operation) with a supply sweep. The gate resistor connects the gate to ground. Drain current creates a voltage across the source resistor. The source becomes positive relative to the gate, so the gate to source voltage becomes negative. ### Find the bias point For negligible gate current, **VGS ≈ −ID × RS**. This relation follows from Ohm's law across the source resistor. The teaching model has **IDSS = 6 mA** and **VGS(off) = −2 V** at 27 °C. These parameters are illustrative. In the saturation region, its drain current follows: **ID = IDSS × (1 − VGS / VGS(off))².** The source resistor and the device equation must agree at the bias point. With 1 kilohm and a 12 V supply, current is approximately 1.131 mA. The gate to source voltage is approximately −1.131 V. A larger source resistor produces a smaller current in this example. ### Supply voltage and operating region Select the low supply view. At low supply voltage, the drain voltage does not support the saturation-region current. The current then depends strongly on the supply voltage. This is different from the nearly flat portion of the curve at higher supply voltage. JFET saturation does not have the same meaning as BJT saturation. The JFET saturation region is the useful region for this current-source example. This model sets channel-length modulation to zero. Its flat current plateau excludes the finite output resistance of a physical JFET. Production JFETs can have large parameter variation. A resistor value that suits this teaching model does not establish a production bias design. Compare this circuit with the [JFET current sink](#jfet-current-sink-example) and the [BJT current mirror](02-BJTs.md#ltspice-example-a-basic-bjt-current-mirror). ## LTspice example: N-channel and P-channel switches This example extends [power switching](#power-switching). Both loads use the same resistance, and both gates receive the same 0 to 5 V pulse. ### Read voltage relative to the source The N-channel source connects to ground. A 5 V gate voltage gives **VGS = +5 V** and turns this device on. Its drain voltage falls toward ground. The load connects between the supply and the drain, so the load receives nearly the full supply voltage. The P-channel source connects to the 5 V supply. A 0 V gate voltage gives **VGS = −5 V** and turns this device on. Its drain voltage rises toward the supply. The load connects between the drain and ground, so the load receives nearly the full supply voltage. A 5 V gate voltage gives the P-channel device **VGS = 0 V** and turns it off. Gate voltage alone does not identify the switch state. ### Compare load current For an ideal switch, load current is **5 V / load resistance**. With a 100-ohm load, the ideal current is 50 mA. The simulated on current is approximately 49.07 mA. Channel resistance and model series resistance account for the difference. These circuits demonstrate polarity and load placement. They do not form a half bridge because their drains connect to separate loads. ### Model limits The symmetric models use thresholds of +2 V and −2 V. They include finite junction capacitance to represent charge storage during switching. The models do not predict production switching losses or a specified device's safe operating area. Inductive loads also require a path for stored energy. Study [gate-drive dynamics](#8-gate-drive-dynamics) and the [body diode](#body-diode) before applying this arrangement to a physical load.
